claims.text: A fixed cost is a cost that does not change with the level of output, such as rent or a manager's salary; a variable cost is a cost that changes directly with output, such as raw materials or packaging.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Total cost is found by adding fixed costs to total variable costs; total variable cost is the variable cost per unit multiplied by the number of units produced.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Average cost per unit is total cost divided by the number of units produced; it falls over a range of output when fixed costs are spread across more units, provided total variable cost rises no faster than output.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Direct costs, such as the flour in each loaf, can be traced to a unit of output, while indirect costs, such as the bakery's rent, are shared across everything the business makes; the same cash amount can sit in either class depending on what causes it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Classifying a cost as fixed or variable tells a business which costs it can escape by producing less and which it must pay whatever happens, which is the first step in judging whether production is worth continuing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost data supports simple decisions such as whether to stop production or continue: if the price covers the variable cost per unit, each sale contributes towards the fixed costs, so a loss-making product may still be worth producing until demand recovers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Continuing to produce when price is below average total cost can still leave the business better off than stopping, because fixed costs continue whether or not anything is made; stopping removes them only when they genuinely end.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost data only measures what the business already knows about; it does not include future price changes, demand shifts or competitor actions, so a cost-based decision is a starting point rather than the last word.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Economies of scale are the falls in average cost per unit that come from producing on a larger scale; internal economies arise inside the growing business itself, while external economies arise from the whole industry or area growing around it. The fall in average cost holds only up to a point, because past a certain size the diseconomies of scale begin to outweigh the savings and average cost rises again.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal economies of scale come in five widely-taught forms: purchasing, where larger orders win bulk discounts; marketing, where the cost of promotion is spread over more sales; financial, where larger businesses usually borrow more cheaply; managerial, where specialists are hired as the business grows; and technical, where larger-scale machinery is affordable.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal economies of scale are what the business can influence through its own growth, while external economies, such as a supplier cluster growing nearby, arrive from outside it and are shared by every producer in the area.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Diseconomies of scale are the rises in average cost per unit that come when a business grows beyond the size it can manage well; like economies, they can be internal, caused by the business's own size, or external, caused by industry-wide congestion.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal diseconomies of scale show up as poor communication, weak coordination and a lack of commitment from employees who feel remote from the business's decisions; each raises average cost by making the larger workforce slower and less reliable than the smaller one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Growth lowers average cost only up to a point: while internal economies of scale outweigh the diseconomies that come with size, cost per unit falls; beyond a certain size diseconomies set in and average cost rises again.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even is the level of output at which total revenue exactly equals total cost, so the business makes neither profit nor loss; below it the business makes a loss, and above it a profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even output is found using the formula fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit, where contribution per unit is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Contribution is the amount each unit sold contributes towards paying the fixed costs; once enough units have been sold for contribution to cover fixed costs in total, the business has reached break-even.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business usually aims to sell beyond break-even because every extra unit sold past that point adds its contribution to profit; the distance between break-even and actual sales is what protects the business from a demand fall.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even output is a number of units, not an amount of money; it is stated as the quantity that must be sold before any profit appears.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A break-even diagram is drawn with output on the horizontal axis and money on the vertical axis; it shows fixed costs as a horizontal line, total cost rising from fixed costs with each unit, and total revenue rising from the origin with price per unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Constructing, completing or amending a break-even diagram follows the same steps whatever the figures: plot the fixed-cost line, add the variable cost to build the total-cost line, draw the revenue line from the origin, and mark the crossing point of revenue with total cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: On a break-even diagram, the crossing point of the total-revenue line with the total-cost line sits directly above the break-even output on the horizontal axis, so the diagram can be amended - for a higher price, say - by redrawing the steeper revenue line and reading off the new crossing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Interpreting a break-even diagram means comparing what the lines show at the business's current output: the vertical gap between the revenue line and the total-cost line is the profit or loss at that output, and the horizontal gap between break-even and current output is the margin of safety.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A break-even diagram is analysed against the situation it describes: a crossing point close to current output signals little protection from a demand fall, while a crossing point far below it signals a business that could lose many sales before losses begin.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even output is calculated as fixed costs divided by contribution per unit; the answer is a quantity of units that must be reached before any profit appears.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: When fixed costs or unit costs change, break-even output changes in a predictable direction: higher fixed costs raise it, a higher price lowers it, and a higher variable cost per unit raises it, provided nothing else moves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The margin of safety is the amount by which current output exceeds break-even output; it is measured in units of output.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The margin of safety is calculated as current output minus break-even output, and it can also be expressed as a percentage of current output; it measures how far sales could fall before losses begin.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A wide margin of safety protects the business from a demand fall, because many sales can be lost before losses begin; a narrow one means a small fall in demand could push the business below break-even.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even analysis supports simple decisions because the effect of a change is a new calculation: a higher price raises contribution per unit, so break-even output falls, provided the higher price does not cost too many sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even analysis helps a business judge a target: a business that knows its break-even output and its capacity can say whether a target profit is reachable, because the units needed for a given profit are fixed costs plus that profit, all divided by contribution per unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even analysis has limitations: it assumes the price and the variable cost per unit stay the same at every output, that fixed costs do not change as output rises, and that everything produced is sold - none of which holds for certain in a real market.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because break-even analysis assumes away demand, a lower break-even output does not by itself mean the business is safe: if demand at the current price is below break-even output, the business makes a loss however low the crossing sits.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A break-even diagram becomes less useful the further output moves from current levels, because costs and prices usually change as a business grows; the analysis is most dependable close to the output it was drawn for.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even analysis and profit are connected through contribution: the analysis itself finds the zero-profit point, and profit or loss at any output is the contribution from that output minus the fixed costs in total.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
